cells.tense: You are carrying what works forward, and the form keeps quietly changing to fit the room without losing the point.
cells.act: find the centre and hold it while things move
cells.ask: In a group you belong to, name the part worth keeping and the part that's gone decorative — then keep the first and retire the second.
cells.core:
You pass things on, and you do it while changing the form to fit the room. The way a family does a holiday, a crew runs a job, a team closes a week — you carry the point of it, drop the trimmings, and people take the version from you. You can do this because the form stays under the meaning. Something is settled underneath, so the surface can move without the thing coming apart.
The adjusting as you go is the part worth keeping. Pick the group where your version of the practice is holding and has drifted from what it was — a routine, a phrase, a standing arrangement. Find one piece that stopped earning its place and retire it. Keep the rest. The balance costs a small correction every few weeks, not a lurch, and it stays yours to make.
cells.sheetLine: You pass on the point, not the wrapping.

cells.tense: You will spend the next season defending how the form has always been done, and the people you're teaching will start slipping out the side door.
cells.act: stop holding up the false thing and watch it come down
cells.ask: Pick one rule you enforce in a group you lead, and let one round of it go unenforced — then watch what actually breaks.
cells.core:
Already, before the meeting, you are braced at the version you'll insist on. The form of the practice has become the whole of it, and anyone who does it differently is wrong rather than just different. What you're holding so tightly was once a living answer to something. Now it's a fence, and the windows in it are sealed.
Stop holding up the part that isn't keeping anyone. Pick a rule you've been enforcing — a way of doing something, a phrase others are expected to use — and let one round of it pass unenforced. Watch what actually breaks. Most of it won't. Underneath, the point of the practice is intact, and you can take it up with both hands once the scaffolding comes away.
cells.sheetLine: The letter has taken the place of the living thing.

cells.tense: You stood at the door of a room full of people and never quite walked in, and no shared form has your name on it now.
cells.act: step back far enough to see the whole arrangement
cells.ask: For a few days, take something you keep working out from scratch, and sketch how it fits together on a page — then leave the page alone.
cells.core:
No practice is holding you. The ones near you seem to be inside something — a faith, a craft, a family way — and you're outside it, smart and self-made and alone with that. You work the same things out fresh each time because nothing carries them for you between rounds. The door isn't as shut as it looks; the furniture inside was made by people too.
Don't reach for the feeling of belonging yet. Instead, take the thing you keep re-deriving for yourself — how you run a project, say, or how you hold a friendship — and step back far enough to sketch how it fits together on a page. Name the pattern in one line. Leave the line alone. What shows up is a form you've been carrying without anything to pass it through.
cells.sheetLine: You keep reinventing what other hands once carried.

cells.tense: You are already teaching something by the way you live in it, and the record in your own head says you're just getting by.
cells.act: add a little or take a little away, and sense the difference
cells.ask: When someone copies how you do something, add or drop one small piece of it next time, and see what shifts in them.
cells.core:
People copy what you do. A habit you run without thinking, a way of talking through a problem, a small ritual around work or food or endings — someone younger or newer or quieter is taking it in. You file it all as just getting by. The transmission is happening anyway, through your hands, and you aren't at the desk as its author.
You don't have to announce anything. The next time someone watches you do something and then does it their own way, that's the thing moving. Take a small piece of how you do it — the timing, the wording, the order — and adjust it one notch. Then see what the notch changed in them. The difference is usually small, and usually lands. Knowing you are the one putting it there is the whole work.

attempts.check: The record supports a capacity, not a biography: the Too Little cell cannot say the person was never taught or was kept outside, only that no shared form is holding them now. A reader might say 'I have plenty of tradition, I just don't practise it' — then the Abstraction act still teaches them how the pattern works. The ask survives a wrong read in every status because each one asks for a bounded act, not a verdict. The sentence that serves me more than them is a lovely abstract line about belonging to something old — cut.
